why_this_tool: Streamlit turns a plain Python script into a clickable app in minutes, so the same file can hold the prototype, its written success criteria and the pilot's evaluation results.
alternatives: Gradio is quicker for a single model input and output demo but weaker for multi-section dashboards; Jupyter suits private exploration but is not something a customer can click through; a custom web frontend on a hosting platform gives full control over the interface but costs far more build time; Langfuse, LangSmith and Braintrust are evaluation and tracing backends that complement rather than replace a demo interface.

setup.do: Check that a supported Python version and a package installer are on the laptop, then create a project folder with a fresh virtual environment.
setup.done_when: The virtual environment is active in the terminal and the project folder is otherwise empty.
setup.why: An isolated environment keeps the prototype reproducible and makes it easy to hand over to a customer engineer later.

setup.do: Install Streamlit into the environment using the command line option and start the built-in hello app.
setup.done_when: The hello demo app opens in the browser on a local address.
setup.why: The hello app confirms the install and the local server work before any of your own code is involved.

setup.do: Skim the get started overview to see how installation, fundamentals and first apps fit together.
setup.done_when: You can name the three parts of the get started section and where the fundamentals live.

source.title: Get started with Streamlit - Streamlit Docs

setup.why: Knowing the map of the documentation saves time when a prototype has only a few days of appetite.

steps.do: Run a first app of your own: create one script that shows a title and a small table, and start it with the streamlit run command.
steps.done_when: Your own script renders in the browser and updates when you save an edit.

source.title: First steps building Streamlit apps - Streamlit Docs

steps.why: This is the whole build loop for a prototype: edit a script, save, see the app update. Getting it under a minute is what makes fast prototyping possible.

steps.do: Create a slider and a text input in the script and watch the whole script rerun on each interaction.
steps.done_when: A counter or timestamp printed in the app changes every time you move the slider.
steps.why: The top to bottom rerun on every interaction is the core execution model, and every later design choice depends on understanding it.

steps.do: Build the prototype fast by following one tutorial to a working chat or form app, with the model call replaced by a stub function so no paid API is needed.
steps.done_when: You can type an input and the app shows a stubbed answer in the page.
steps.why: Starting from a tutorial pattern gets a clickable demo in front of the customer in hours. A stubbed response keeps it laptop-only while the interface and flow are tested.

steps.do: Configure session state and caching so the conversation history survives reruns and the stubbed call is not repeated for the same input.
steps.done_when: Earlier inputs stay visible after new interactions and a repeated input returns instantly.
steps.why: Without state the prototype forgets everything on each click, and without caching a real model call would be paid for again on every rerun.

steps.do: Write a header block at the top of the app that states whether this is a prototype, a POC or a pilot and the one question it is meant to answer, using the text elements.
steps.done_when: The first thing visible in the app is the stage name and a single question in one sentence.
steps.why: A prototype proves the idea is worth pursuing, a POC proves it is feasible on the customer's data, and a pilot proves it holds up with real users. Putting the stage on screen stops the audience expecting more than the stage proves.

steps.do: Write an appetite and scope panel with a caption giving the time box and end date, the one workflow that is in scope and a short list of what is out of scope.
steps.done_when: The app shows an end date, one in-scope workflow and at least three explicit out-of-scope items.
steps.why: Fixing the appetite before building forces the problem to be narrowed to fit the time, not the time stretched to fit the problem.

steps.do: Write the success criteria as a row of metric elements, each with a current value, a target threshold and a delta against that target.
steps.done_when: Three or more metrics are displayed, each showing a value and whether it is above or below its target.
steps.why: A criterion is measurable only when it has a number and a pass line agreed before the build. Metrics make the go or no-go evidence readable at a glance.

steps.do: Load a fixed set of evaluation cases from a local file into a data editor, record pass or fail and a note per case, and save the edited table back to a dated file.
steps.done_when: A new dated results file appears on disk after you mark cases and press save.
steps.why: This is the evaluation loop of a pilot: the same cases, judged the same way, persisted after every change so results are evidence, not memory.

steps.do: Compare two saved evaluation runs side by side in a dataframe and a simple bar chart, and feed the pass rate into the metrics row.
steps.done_when: Selecting two run files shows per-case differences and the metrics row updates to the newer run's pass rate.
steps.why: Comparing runs shows whether a prompt or logic change actually moved the criteria. That is the signal a customer needs for the decision.

steps.do: Read the deployment concepts page and list what the pilot app would need to be shared beyond your laptop, using a second local browser session as the substitute for a hosted deployment.
steps.done_when: You have a written checklist of dependencies, secrets and access needs, and two browser sessions show independent state.
steps.why: A pilot has real users, so you need to know how dependencies, secrets and sessions behave once the app leaves your machine. No listed page gives a local serving walkthrough, so this is a reading step.

steps.do: Reproduce the app from scratch: declare pinned dependencies in a requirements file, create a fresh virtual environment, install from the file and run the app again.
steps.done_when: The app starts in the fresh environment and the evaluation view shows the same pass rate as before.
steps.why: A pilot that only runs on the builder's laptop is not evidence. A pinned environment lets the customer or a teammate rerun the evaluation and get the same numbers.

steps.do: Register and mount a small custom component for reviewer feedback, such as a thumbs rating with a comment, and write its returned value into the evaluation results table.
steps.done_when: Submitting feedback through the mounted component adds a row to the saved results and changes the displayed metrics.
steps.why: Packaging the feedback control as a registered component makes it reusable across pilots. It also moves the app toward a production-like setup where real users feed the evaluation loop directly.
